intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC1DN7) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the NDUFV2 gene.

paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial complex I deficiency nuclear type 7 (MC1DN7) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in NDUFV2, which encodes the 24-kD subunit of mitochondrial respiratory chain complex I. Affected individuals have shown early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with trunk hypotonia and encephalopathy, or Leigh syndrome without cardiac involvement (Benit et al., 2003; Cameron et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: In 3 sibs from a consanguineous family with MC1DN7, Benit et al. (2003) identified a homozygous 4-bp deletion in intron 2 of the NDUFV2 gene (IVS2+5_+8delGTAA). They detected it by denaturing high performance liquid chromatography and sequence analysis. The mutation altered the consensus splice-donor site of exon 2 and resulted in a 70% decrease in NDUFV2 protein and complex I deficiency.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sibs with MC1DN7 who had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and brain atrophy, Cameron et al. (2015) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the NDUFV2 gene by whole-exome sequencing. One allele was the previously reported intronic mutation (c.IVS2+1delGTAA). The other was a novel insertion (c.669_670insG) predicted to cause a frameshift (Ser224ValfsTer3). Screening of 10 probands with complex I deficiency from different families revealed a second, consanguineous family in which the affected sibs were homozygous for the c.IVS2+1delGTAA mutation. These 3 affected sibs (of 5) had Leigh syndrome without cardiac involvement.

paragraphs.text: Cameron et al. (2015) noted that the same homozygous intronic NDUFV2 genotype was associated with different phenotypes in different families. Previously reported families had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, trunk hypotonia, and encephalopathy (see Benit et al., 2003). In contrast, the affected sibs they studied presented with Leigh syndrome and no cardiac involvement.
